title: What AI-assisted testing caught—and missed—in my Slime Soccer-inspired browser game
author: StandAble2695
selftext:
I’m building Slime Kickoff, a free browser football game inspired by classic Slime Soccer. Most of its code and much of its design were developed with OpenAI Codex, which also helped prepare this write-up. It uses JavaScript physics, Canvas 2D procedural art and Web Audio effects.



The workflow has been small changes followed by simulations using the actual game engine, targeted regression checks and browser tests. Those checks help with reproducible bugs, but they cannot establish whether a newcomer understands heading or wants another match.



One useful lesson was separating result recording from the celebration that presents it. A match-ending goal and the normal end callback can deliver the same result at different points. Updating progress independently in both paths risks awarding it twice; waiting for the animation to finish risks losing progress when someone leaves early. Both paths now use one match-local gate that records a confirmed result once and returns the same receipt for duplicate delivery. Regression checks cover duplicate callbacks and leaving during the final celebration.



I’d like feedback on the part automation cannot judge: controlling the ball against the first bot. The accompanying clip uses simulated controls against the actual bot, with a labelled replay. It is a demonstration, not footage of a human playtest.



Could you try one full Rookie match, win or lose, and share your final score and the first moment that felt confusing? If you choose a rematch, what prompted it—or what stopped you?



Play with arrow keys or touch, without an account or download:

[https://hopbold-playground-mj.mjanssondk.chatgpt.site/?challenge=rookie](https://hopbold-playground-mj.mjanssondk.chatgpt.site/?challenge=rookie)



The playtest is free; the longer-term plan is optional cosmetics.
